topics.title: Accessibility (a11y) Fundamentals
topics.summary: Build pages everyone can use: semantic HTML, labels, alt text, contrast and headings first.
topics.description:
**Accessibility** (written *a11y*: a + 11 letters + y) means people with disabilities - blind, low vision, deaf, motor-impaired, cognitive - can perceive, operate and understand your site. It also helps everyone: mobile users in sunlight, people with a broken arm, keyboard power users.

### The first rule of ARIA
"If you can use a native HTML element, use it." Native elements come with roles, keyboard handling and states for free.

### The practical checklist
| Area | What to do |
|---|---|
| Structure | Use landmarks (header, nav, main, footer) and a heading hierarchy |
| Images | Meaningful `alt`; `alt=""` for decoration |
| Forms | Every control has a `<label>`; group with fieldset/legend; helpful error text |
| Links & buttons | Descriptive text; links navigate, buttons act |
| Language | `lang` attribute |
| Media | Captions, transcripts; no autoplay with sound |
| Colour | Contrast ratio ≥ 4.5:1 for text; do not rely on colour alone |
| Keyboard | Everything usable with Tab/Enter/Space; visible focus |
| Motion | Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` |
| Zoom | Do not block pinch zoom; content reflows at 200% |

### WCAG
The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (A, AA, AAA) are the standard. Most laws require **AA**. Principles: **POUR** - Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.

### Test it
- Tab through the page with only a keyboard.
- Use a screen reader (NVDA, VoiceOver).
- Browser DevTools Accessibility pane, Lighthouse, axe.
keyPoints: Native semantic HTML solves most accessibility needs.
All functionality must work with a keyboard.
Provide text alternatives: alt, labels, captions.
Contrast 4.5:1 for normal text (WCAG AA).
WCAG principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.
pitfalls: Using a div with onclick instead of a button.
Conveying meaning with colour only (red error with no text).
Removing the focus outline with outline:none and no replacement.

topics.title: ARIA: roles, states & properties
topics.summary: WAI-ARIA adds accessibility information that native HTML cannot express, for custom widgets.
topics.description:
**ARIA** (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of attributes that tell assistive technology what a custom UI element is and what state it is in. ARIA changes **only the accessibility tree**, not behaviour or appearance.

### The five rules in short
1. Prefer native HTML (`<button>` over `<div role="button">`).
2. Do not change native semantics unnecessarily.
3. All interactive ARIA controls must be keyboard operable.
4. Never use `role="presentation"` or `aria-hidden="true"` on focusable elements.
5. All interactive elements need an accessible name.

### Three attribute groups
| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Roles** (what it is) | `role="tablist"`, `dialog`, `alert`, `navigation`, `button` |
| **Properties** (relationships/labels) | `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-controls` |
| **States** (changing) | `aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, `aria-checked`, `aria-hidden`, `aria-disabled`, `aria-live` |

### Frequently used
- `aria-label="Close"` - name for an icon-only button.
- `aria-labelledby="id"` - name from another element.
- `aria-describedby="id"` - extra description (e.g. an error hint).
- `aria-expanded="true|false"` - disclosure/menu state.
- `aria-live="polite"` - announce updates (status messages).
- `role="alert"` - important, immediate announcement.
- `aria-current="page"` - current link in navigation.

### Landmarks
Use `<nav aria-label="Main">` when there are several navs so users can tell them apart.

Wrong ARIA is worse than no ARIA - always test with a screen reader.
keyPoints: First rule: use native HTML before ARIA.
ARIA only changes semantics, not behaviour - you must add the keyboard support.
aria-label / labelledby provide accessible names.
aria-expanded and aria-live communicate changing state.
Never hide focusable elements with aria-hidden.
pitfalls: Adding role="button" to a div but no keyboard handling.
aria-label on non-interactive elements that ignore it (div/span without role).

interview.q: What is the first rule of ARIA?
interview.a: Do not use ARIA if a native HTML element or attribute with the needed semantics already exists.

topics.title: Global Attributes
topics.summary: id, class, style, title, hidden, lang, dir, contenteditable, draggable, tabindex and more work on any element.
topics.description:
**Global attributes** can be put on **any** HTML element.

| Attribute | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `id` | Unique identifier (fragment links, JS, labels) |
| `class` | One or more CSS/JS hooks |
| `style` | Inline CSS |
| `title` | Advisory tooltip text |
| `lang` / `dir` | Language and text direction |
| `hidden` | Hide the element (like display:none) |
| `tabindex` | Keyboard focus order |
| `accesskey` | Keyboard shortcut |
| `contenteditable` | Make content editable by the user |
| `spellcheck` | Enable/disable spell checking |
| `draggable` | Allow drag and drop |
| `translate` | Whether content should be translated |
| `data-*` | Custom data (next topic) |
| `role`, `aria-*` | Accessibility |
| `inert` | Make a subtree non-interactive |
| `popover` | Popover behaviour |
| `autofocus`, `enterkeyhint`, `inputmode` | Input-related hints |
| `is`, `slot`, `part` | Web components |

### Notes
- `id` must be unique and should not contain spaces. Start with a letter for CSS convenience.
- `hidden` is easily overridden by CSS `display` rules.
- `contenteditable="true"` turns a div into a rich text area - great for prototypes, but real apps need validation and sanitization.
- `inert` is excellent for disabling background content behind a custom modal.
- Inline `style` has high specificity; keep styles in CSS files.
keyPoints: Global attributes apply to every HTML element.
id is unique; class is reusable.
hidden, inert and contenteditable change behaviour without JS.
lang and dir set language/direction for any subtree.
data-* stores custom values.
pitfalls: Relying on title for essential information (not available on touch/keyboard).
Using style attributes everywhere and fighting specificity later.

topics.title: Custom data-* Attributes
topics.summary: Store small custom values on elements and read them with dataset in JavaScript or attr() / attribute selectors in CSS.
topics.description:
HTML does not let you invent random attributes (`
` is invalid). For custom data use **`data-*` attributes**: `data-` followed by your own lowercase name. ```html
  • Mango
    • ``` ### Reading in JavaScript The `dataset` object maps names to **camelCase**: ```js const li = document.querySelector('li'); li.dataset.id; // "42" li.dataset.inStock; // "true" (data-in-stock -> inStock) li.dataset.color = 'orange'; // sets data-color="orange" ``` Values are always **strings** - convert with `Number()` or `JSON.parse()`. ### Using in CSS - Attribute selectors: `[data-category="fruit"] { color: green }` - Show a value: `li::after { content: attr(data-id) }` ### Good uses - Passing IDs to JavaScript (e.g. `data-product-id` on a button). - State flags for styling (`data-state="open"`). - Configuration for small widgets. ### What not to put there - Content that users or search engines must see (put real text in the HTML). - Secrets or sensitive data - visible to everyone. - Large JSON blobs - use a script tag (`type="application/json"`).
keyPoints: Custom attribute names must start with data- and be lowercase.
JavaScript reads them via element.dataset (camelCased).
Values are strings.
CSS can select by [data-*] and show values with attr().
Never store secrets in data attributes.
pitfalls: Expecting numbers or booleans - they are strings ("false" is truthy!).
Putting important content only in data attributes.
Using uppercase letters in the attribute name.

interview.q: How do you read data-user-id in JavaScript?
interview.a: element.dataset.userId - hyphenated names become camelCase and the value is a string.

interview.q: Why use data attributes instead of custom attributes?
interview.a: Arbitrary attributes are invalid HTML; data-* is the standard-approved way to attach custom data.

topics.title: Microdata & JSON-LD Structured Data
topics.summary: Describe your content in a machine-readable way so search engines can show rich results.
topics.description:
**Structured data** adds explicit meaning to your content using the **schema.org** vocabulary. Search engines read it to build *rich results*: star ratings, recipe cards, event dates, FAQs, product prices, breadcrumbs. ### Three syntaxes | Syntax | How | |---|---| | **JSON-LD** (recommended) | A ` ``` ### Microdata ```html
Laptop 55000
``` ### Rules - The data **must match** what users see on the page. - Validate with Google's Rich Results Test or schema.org validator. - Common types: `Article`, `Product`, `Recipe`, `Event`, `FAQPage`, `Organization`, `BreadcrumbList`.
keyPoints: Structured data uses the schema.org vocabulary.
JSON-LD in script type="application/ld+json" is the preferred format.
Microdata uses itemscope, itemtype and itemprop on visible elements.
It enables rich results; it does not guarantee them.
Markup must reflect visible page content.
pitfalls: Marking up content that is not visible on the page.
Invalid JSON (trailing commas) in the LD+JSON block.

interview.q: What is JSON-LD and why is it preferred?
interview.a: A JSON format for schema.org data placed in a script tag, separated from visible markup and easy to maintain; recommended by Google.
itemscope, itemtype and itemprop - added to visible elements to describe items and their properties.
